mcqs.question: In the double-checked locking skeleton, what's the actual defect being fixed at step 3?
options: A reference to the singleton can become visible to another thread before the constructor finishes writing its fields
The synchronized block executes too many times, once per call
The null check itself throws a NullPointerException on the first call
The class fails to compile without an explicit no-args constructor
mcqs.explanation: The defect is a reordering hazard — the object's reference can be observed before its constructor's writes are, letting a reader see a half-built instance. The synchronized block runs correctly, the null check throws nothing by itself, and no explicit constructor requirement exists.

mcqs.question: Without volatile, why can a second thread see a non-null instance that points to a half-constructed object?
options: Because synchronized blocks in Java never actually acquire a real lock
Because the compiler or CPU can reorder the reference assignment ahead of the constructor's writes finishing
Because Java always runs static field assignments on a background thread
Because the second thread reads instance before the first thread has even entered the synchronized block
mcqs.explanation: Without volatile, nothing stops the compiler or CPU from making the reference assignment visible before the constructor's field writes are visible to other threads. synchronized blocks do acquire real locks, static assignments run on the initializing thread, and this bug is unrelated to entry timing into the synchronized block.

mcqs.question: What specifically changed in Java 5's memory model (JSR-133) that made the volatile fix reliable?
options: Java 5 removed the synchronized keyword in favor of volatile entirely
Java 5 made all fields volatile by default
Java 5 gave a volatile write a full happens-before guarantee, so every write before it in program order becomes visible to a subsequent reader
Java 5 introduced garbage collection for the first time
mcqs.explanation: JSR-133 strengthened volatile into a full happens-before edge, which is exactly what closes the DCL reordering gap. synchronized was never removed, fields aren't volatile by default, and garbage collection long predates Java 5.

mcqs.question: Why is it wrong to assume double-checked locking is safe in every language just because Java fixed it in Java 5?
options: Because double-checked locking was never actually broken in any language, including pre-Java-5 Java
Because Java 5's fix requires internet connectivity to take effect
Because every modern language automatically provides Java's exact volatile semantics
Because the fix is specific to Java's memory model and volatile guarantee — other languages or older compilers may lack an equivalent ordering guarantee
mcqs.explanation: The fix lives in Java's specific memory model revision and its volatile keyword; it says nothing about other languages' guarantees. Pre-Java-5 Java genuinely had this bug, the fix has nothing to do with connectivity, and not every language provides an equivalent to volatile's ordering semantics.
